content.title: Logistic Regression & The Sigmoid Function
content.explanation:
• Beginner-friendly explanation.
• Despite its misleading name, Logistic Regression is actually a classification algorithm, not a regression one.
• It answers Yes/No questions: Is this email spam?
• Will this customer churn?
• Does this patient have diabetes?

content.title: The Sigmoid Curve
content.explanation: This is the 'giant squasher' we talked about. Notice how it takes any extreme value and gracefully bends it so it never crosses 0% or 100%.

content.title: Decision Trees: The Architecture of Logic
content.explanation:
• Beginner-friendly explanation.
• A Decision Tree is simply an automated flowchart.
• Real-world intuition.
• Think of playing '20 Questions' with a friend.
• A Decision Tree does the exact same thing with data.

content.title: Decision Trees
content.explanation: Here is the flowchart logic in action. The model starts at the root question and simply follows the True/False branches down to the final prediction.

content.prompt: We just learned that Decision Trees can grow too deep and memorize the training data. This is called Overfitting. If a tree just memorizes the specific practice data, what will happen when we give it brand new, unseen data to predict in the real world?

questions.question: In a dataset of 1,000 transactions, only 10 are fraudulent. A model simply predicts 'Not Fraud' for everything. What is its Accuracy?
questions.expectedAnswer: 99% (990/1000). This proves why Accuracy is a terrible metric for highly imbalanced datasets.

questions.question: If you want to ensure you catch EVERY single fraudulent transaction, even if it means falsely flagging some normal ones, which metric should you optimize: Precision or Recall?
questions.expectedAnswer: Recall. Optimizing Recall minimizes False Negatives (missed frauds).

content.title: Understanding Classification Metrics
content.explanation:
• Beginner-friendly explanation.
• Classification metrics are the report cards for your model.
• • Precision: Of everything the model CLAIMED was positive, how many actually were?
• • F1 Score: The harmonic mean that balances Precision and Recall into a single number.
• Real-world intuition.

content.title: The Confusion Matrix
content.explanation: This 2x2 grid summarizes exactly where the model succeeded and where it failed, making it much more detailed and useful than just a single 'Accuracy' score.

content.title: Precision vs Recall
content.explanation: The sniper (Precision) only fires when 100% certain, avoiding false alarms but missing some targets. The massive net (Recall) catches every single target, but hauls in a bunch of garbage (false alarms) too.

content.question: You are designing an AI for a hospital to detect a deadly, highly contagious virus. A False Positive means a healthy person gets quarantined for a day. A False Negative means an infected person goes to a concert and infects thousands. Which metric should you optimize?

options.feedback: Wrong! If you optimize Precision, the AI will only flag people it's 100% sure about, meaning it will miss mild cases (False Negatives) who will go out and infect the city!
Exactly! In a deadly pandemic, you want a 'massive net' (High Recall). It's better to accidentally quarantine a few healthy people than to let a deadly virus escape.

challenge.explanation: This code demonstrates calculating core classification metrics using scikit-learn. The model achieves 80% accuracy but has higher precision and recall for the positive class. The F1 score shows a balanced performance between precision and recall.
challenge.hint: Remember that scikit-learn's functions automatically calculate these metrics when given true and predicted labels. The output will show how well the model performed across different metrics.
challenge.question: Calculate metrics for a sample confusion matrix
challenge.solution:
# Calculated values
# Accuracy: 0.80
# Precision: 0.83
# Recall: 0.86
# F1 Score: 0.85
challenge.starterCode:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

# Sample predictions and true labels
y_true = [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0]  # 1 = positive class
y_pred = [1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0]

# Calculate metrics
accuracy = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
precision = precision_score(y_true, y_pred)
recall = recall_score(y_true, y_pred)
f1 = f1_score(y_true, y_pred)

# Print results
print(f'Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}')
print(f'Precision: {precision:.2f}')
print(f'Recall: {recall:.2f}')
print(f'F1 Score: {f1:.2f}')

content.title: Random Forest: The Wisdom of Crowds
content.explanation:
• Beginner-friendly explanation.
• Real-world intuition.
• Why the concept matters.
• Random Forests are the Swiss Army Knife of Machine Learning.
• They are the default 'first algorithm' that most data scientists reach for in industry.

content.title: Random Forest: The Wisdom of Crowds
content.explanation: Each tree sees a different random subset of data and features. Their individual predictions may be imperfect, but the aggregated majority vote is remarkably accurate and stable—this is the power of Ensemble Learning.

content.title: Support Vector Machines (SVM): Maximizing the Margin
content.explanation:
• Beginner-friendly explanation.
• The wider the margin, the more confident the model is about its classification.
• Real-world intuition.
• Imagine you are building a fence between a dog park and a cat park.
• SVM builds the widest possible fence.

content.title: Support Vector Machines (SVM): Maximizing the Margin
content.explanation: Notice the wide gap (margin) between the two classes. The data points sitting exactly on the dotted margin lines are the Support Vectors—they define the boundary. SVM maximizes this gap for the most confident possible classification.

content.title: ROC & AUC: The Ultimate Balancer
content.explanation:
• Beginner-friendly explanation.
• AUC = 0.5 means the model is guessing randomly (worthless).
• AUC = 1.0 means it is a perfect classifier.
• Real-world intuition.
• Imagine you are tuning a metal detector at the airport.

content.title: ROC and AUC
content.explanation: This curve visualizes the exact tradeoff we discussed. A perfect model hugs the top left, while the diagonal line represents completely random guessing.
